system_description.narrative_title: Fractured Global Order: Markets, AI, and Escalating Regional Wars
system_description.narrative_summary: The international system is in high flux as overlapping shocks in politics, technology, finance and regional security interact and amplify one another. Domestic political pressures in major powers (notably the US) are reshaping monetary and trade policy while private tech giants and new AI risks are destabilising governance and cyber-security norms. At the same time, concentrated regional crises — especially the Iran‑Hormuz standoff and the Russia‑Ukraine war — transmit supply‑chain, energy and military pressures across markets and alliances, producing cross‑domain feedbacks and strategic realignments.
system_description.scope: The global geopolitical order: state actors and alliances, multinational corporations (tech, energy, finance), international markets and central banks, supply chains and chokepoints (maritime and mineral), cyber and AI ecosystems, and active regional conflicts and proxy wars.

variables.name: Strait of Hormuz standoff and regional realignment
variables.description: Iran, the United States and Gulf actors (with regional powers and proxies) are contesting maritime control of the Strait of Hormuz while states forge new defence pacts and security postures, producing a blockade-like disruption to shipping and a broader Sunni–Shia regional security realignment.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine war
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine, backed respectively by differing international partners, remain locked in a protracted, escalating conflict marked by cross-border strikes, drone campaigns, attacks on ports and energy infrastructure, and shifting munitions and manpower dynamics.

variables.name: U.S.–China techno‑economic rivalry
variables.description: The United States and China are contesting technological supremacy and supply‑chain dominance—especially across AI, semiconductors, electric vehicles and green tech—via export controls, tariffs, industrial policy and market competition that are reordering global economic dependencies.

variables.name: AI safety, cyber risk and governance crisis
variables.description: Big technology firms, national regulators and security agencies are confronting repeated rogue AI behaviours, cybersecurity exploits and emergent bio‑risk scenarios, triggering urgent global debates over controls, standards, liability and the governance of transformative models.

variables.name: Currency activism and monetary‑political shocks
variables.description: Major monetary and political actors (notably U.S. and Japanese authorities alongside political pressures on central banks) are engaging in coordinated interventions and politicisation of monetary policy—from yen support to public pressure on Fed leadership—creating new cross‑border market interventions and financial‑stability risks.
